vignette: Arthur had never expected violence from Eleanor. He had come to believe that intimacy was a quiet agreement, until the nights grew heavy with sudden strikes. It was not a linear account he could trace, only a series of sharp, unconnected moments: a hand clamped over his mouth during a late argument, a shoulder slamming into a doorway as he turned away, the terrifying press of her body against his in the dark. Now, at sixty-eight, he could not tell a clear story of what happened even to himself. What remained were snapshots that accumulated on their own. Remembering what happened during the frightening event is just like looking at photographs of it in his mind-crisp, silent frames of her raised fist, the floorboards tilting beneath his feet, the cold brass of the door handle pressed hard against his ribs. Sometimes the images vanished entirely, and he finds himself feeling the full emotional intensity of the event without any clear image or memory, a sudden pressure in his chest that demands nothing and explains nothing. As the years passed, Arthur's beliefs about how the world works have been completely destroyed. He began watching other people closely, especially their hands and the set of their jaws, searching for the hidden threat. He is certain that beneath polite smiles, people are not what they seem, capable of turning at any moment. Alongside this distrust, he has come to believe he is inadequate, no matter how carefully he moves or how well he prepares. His wife, Margaret, has observed how he avoids wearing similar clothes to the wool and thick cotton he wore during those years, changing fabrics and cuts to create a subtle boundary against the past. He tries hard to control his emotions, maintaining a steady, unbroken composure, and he never allows himself to feel or express anger, keeping his own stillness carefully aligned with the quiet hours of his life. His work as a psychologist provides the specific setting where these habits take root. In his quiet office at the university clinic, Arthur conducts sessions with careful precision. When a female patient sits alone across from him, he keeps the space between them exact, his shoulders squared, feeling the familiar tension of being alone with women. He finds it harder to feel safe at night than during the day, and the quiet of his bedroom often gives way to waking alertness; he rises to check the locks, listens for footsteps, and ensures the house has not shifted. Crowded spaces press against him as well. At department meetings, the murmur of colleagues and the close proximity of bodies trigger a familiar overstimulation, making him feel as though the walls might close in. Even transportation tests him. A bicycle leaning against a wall or a rider passing too close sends a flicker of alarm through him, his body bracing against the familiar impact. For months, Arthur navigated his days by these co-existing patterns, maintaining the demeanor expected of a man who spends his life interpreting others. But lately, the photographs in his mind are multiplying, and the emotional weight without images is growing heavier. He finds himself skipping evening walks, declining social gatherings, and sitting rigidly in his car when navigating traffic. What finally brought him to seek help was a Tuesday afternoon in his practice. A young female patient reached across to adjust his pen, her fingers brushing his wrist. Arthur flinched, his breath catching, and in that sudden stillness he recognized how closely his body and his mind now run alongside each other. He is hoping to find a way to quiet the constant watching, to let the photographs settle, and to step out of the careful architecture he has built, even if the world remains as unpredictable as ever.
